sections.title: The strategy of the proof, followed through the Lean text

sentences.text: The proof in src derives the five theorems of Main.lean from one inequality.
The first theorem states that a Dirichlet L-function has no zero with real part above 1/2, and the other four follow from it.
The inequality says that a weighted sum over the prime powers up to x, with its main terms subtracted, is at most x^(1/2 + cε) for all x between Y and Y^(3/2).
This holds for every small ε > 0 and for arbitrarily large Y, with a constant c that depends on neither ε nor Y.
The proof gets the inequality by bounding the slope of one lattice from two sides.
A divisibility inequality bounds that slope, together with a height term, from above by m times a main term, where m is the number of lifts in a chain between unitary groups.
The author's note calls them theta lifts.
A slope inequality bounds the same slope from below.
The two bounds leave error terms of about x/m and about m for the weighted sum, and the proof assumes that m lies in a window around √x, where both terms are about √x.
This document follows that route through the Lean text.

It goes from Main.lean down to the upper bound for one lift and the lower bound for the maps into the lattice, and then through the assembly of the conditions and the branches that supply the premises.
For each step it names the theorem that carries the step, says what the theorem states and how much of its proof was read, and gives the number of declarations that the theorem rests on.
A language model, Claude, read the route in one session on 23 and 24 November 2026.
Seven further runs of the same model each read one branch and reported back.
A table below names the seven readings, and a section names the reading behind a sentence that comes from a report.
A sentence without a named reading reports what this session read.
On 24 November two more runs of the same model compared the nine steps with the Lean text, one for each half of the route, and their twenty findings are worked in.
On the same day Gemini, a model of another maker, compared four parts of this document and the list of claims in CLAIMS.md with the Lean text.
Four runs of the first model compared its findings with the Lean text, and the findings that held are worked in.
That list gives the tally.
No mathematician has checked the readings, and Lean was not run for this document.

Mathlib and Lean's library are outside the count.

A premise is a hypothesis of a theorem.
A premise is supplied when a call of the theorem passes a proof of it.
A closed theorem is a theorem that takes no premises.
A record is a Lean structure.
A bundle is a record whose fields are propositions, so a field of it is one premise.
A datum is a value of the code's record D7, which D7.md opens.
It holds a host, lattices, maps and the number m of lifts.

The slope of a lattice is the code's number mu.

Statement.lean defines the covolume covol of a lattice in a Euclidean space as the square root of the Gram determinant of a basis, the degree as minus the logarithm of the covolume, and the slope as the degree divided by the rank.
The largest slope muMax is the supremum of the slopes of the nonzero sublattices.
The smallest slope muMin is the infimum of the slopes of the quotients of the lattice by its saturated proper sublattices.

For a Hermitian lattice over a number field K the definition muDef in StatementPl.lean sets mu to twice the slope of the lattice, minus log 2, plus the quotient of log |d_K| by the degree of K over the rational numbers, where d_K is the discriminant of K.
The height of a map is the code's number htMap in the file of muDef.
It is the mean, over the infinite places of K, of the logarithm of the squared operator norm of the map.
The number h of a word of a datum is a different number.
It is a real field of the datum, the condition WordFacts requires that the height of the map of the word, when the map is not zero, is at most h, and in a family a formula named hExpl6 gives h.
A link is one of the conditions on a family in GlobalTheoremInputs.lean whose names begin with Link.

Its timeline has 20 numbered entries.

The seven parallel readings are these.
Each brief asked for the Lean text only, and each report marked its own guesses.

The five theorems follow from one statement, that a Dirichlet L-function has no zero with real part above 1/2.
The Lean statement sets aside the trivial character at s = 1.
That statement follows from an upper bound x^θ, for every θ above 1/2, for a weighted prime sum Gm x on the intervals from Y to Y^(3/2), for arbitrarily large Y.
The sum has its main terms subtracted.
The step is a Landau argument.
The sum Gm is a weighted sum of the prime sums of a finite set of characters, the wanted characters.
The proof places them among the characters of an auxiliary abelian field, the host.
A sum over a subgroup removes the characters that are nontrivial on it, and the proof bounds the prime sum of each remaining unwanted character separately.
The host depends on two primes q and d.

A count of zeros and a mean square bound show that at least half of the candidates for q, and then at least half of the candidates for d, give every such character a prime sum of at most y^(1/2 + ε/2) for the y from Y to Y^A, where A ≥ 1 is an exponent that the caller chooses.
The sections below call the wanted characters kept and the unwanted characters that remain the other characters.
The sum over all characters of the auxiliary field equals an arithmetic quantity ASK minus its main term, by finite Fourier inversion.
ASK is bounded through the slope of a lattice.
A divisibility inequality DIV bounds the slope from above, and a slope inequality SlopeIneq bounds it from below by a mean over further lattices.
A third condition puts a quantity below the slope of each further lattice, and ASK is at most that quantity plus a loss.
Both bounds concern linear maps into that lattice, one map for each word of a datum.
A pairing of each word factors through a chain of m kernels between spaces that carry unitary groups.
The ranks are k + j(t + 1) for j from 0 to m − 1 and k + m(t + 1) − 1 on the last space, where k and t are two natural numbers of the datum.
The first m − 2 kernels are composed one after the other, the last two are composed inside a finite sum, and one more linear map follows.
This document does not record how the pairing is tied to the map.
The main term of the upper bound holds one term a·log a − a − a·logOm for each lift and each top place, where a is the top weight at that place and logOm is a constant of the host.
For one lift, interlacing weights and a hook product bound a sum over its weights by a·log a − a plus an error term.
The lower bound applies a general statement about several maps into one lattice.
It takes two bounds on products of matrices of the maps and one bound on their number of rows, which a link supplies for a second set of maps, and it takes a family with many words.
A premise says that such families exist, and this document does not follow where that premise is proved.
By this document's interpretation the bounds say that the maps are nearly isometries after scaling, in the mean over the family, and that the images of the maps fill the target evenly.
After a division the two bounds leave error terms of about x/m and about m for the weighted sum, and a further term of about √x that does not depend on m.
The proof assumes that m lies between x^(1/2 − ε) and x^(1/2 + ε/2).
With further premises on the numbers of the error, that keeps every term at most 4·x^(1/2 + 13ε/8) and gives the exponent 1/2 + cε.
The sections below have names and no numbers, and the word step means one of these nine.
The four parts of the Landau argument are called stages.
Each step has a short name for use where its number alone says too little.
Step — Short name
1 — Zero-free half-plane
2 — Landau argument
3 — Host field and kept characters
4 — Fourier inversion to ASK
5 — Two bounds on one slope
6 — Chain of kernels
7 — Upper bound for one lift

9 — Window for m
The section on the two bounds covers steps 4, 5 and 9.
Two sections cover the upper bound and step 7, one covers the chain of step 6, and one covers the lower bound of step 8.
Further branches supply the premises of this route.
One proves a bound on lengths of Galois cohomology groups, which the code calls VWin.
One proves the existence of Galois representations, which the code calls Row.
The largest one builds a record of 46 fields, five of data and 41 conditions on the families.
One of the conditions says that the chains of lifts exist, and a covolume bound feeds the record.

sections.title: What the note says about the strategy

sentences.text: The note gives the idea in one paragraph and a timeline.
This session read the PDF directly.

The note says that "In Stepanov's argument resolving Riemann over function fields one uses a divisor involving multiplicity" and that the argument "is a descendant of Stepanov's, but multiplicity is hard to find over the integers".
Entry 5 of the timeline switches to the sum Σ Λ(n)·(X/n − 1) over n ≤ X, minus X log X, plus (1 + γ)·X.
The Lean definition Gz, which the section on the prime sum gives, is this expression, and it is the part of the sum Gm of step 2 that belongs to the trivial character.
Entry 7 speaks of "GGP periods, with values 0, 1 meaning interlacing weights".
Entry 8 reads "Iterated theta lifts U(X_0) → U(X_1) → ··· → U(X_m) between totally definite unitary groups, π ↦ π ⊞ μ_j[t], wins multiplicity m.
Time to take m like √X".

Entries 9, 10, 12, 13 and 16 name the norms of the lifts with divisibility "via Chowla-Selberg, Weyl, and Siegel mass", a lower bound on the divisibility of the m-fold lift, a seesaw that makes the period of the iterated lift a Bessel period, the Bost slope inequality, and the "approximate orthogonality of the columns of the integral structure".
Entry 17 speaks of classes in H¹(𝒪_E[1/ℓ], ℚ_ℓ/ℤ_ℓ(−e)) and "a significant weakening of Vandiver".

The author writes that Claude provided the timeline, that parts of it paraphrase a summary "which might make zero sense", and that he presents the argument "before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics".
A section below names an entry where the Lean text matches it by a formula or by its names.

sections.title: From a bound on intervals to zero-freeness
What zero_free_all_of_green_v_win states and how it splits

sentences.text: The theorem in TopPlug.lean takes Green, VWin and the existence of one record of type HypsAlt.
It concludes ZeroFreeAll, which unfolds into Mathlib terms.
For every primitive Dirichlet character ψ and every s with real part above 1/2, DirichletCharacter.LFunction ψ.χ s ≠ 0.
The theorem imprimitive, which rests on 7 declarations, extends the conclusion to all characters through the Euler factors, with the trivial character at s = 1 set aside.
Its proof, which this session read, writes the L-function of a character as the L-function of its primitive character times finitely many Euler factors, and no factor is zero for real part above 1/2.
The proof is one line.
It calls zeroFreeAll_of_topG, which rests on 791 declarations and contains the first two rows of the next table, and it passes the last two rows to it as supplies.
This session read the proofs of all four rows in full, without the theorems that they call.
Part — Theorem — What it gives — Rests on
Landau step — formB — an upper bound for a prime sum on intervals gives zero-freeness — 108
Main inequality — level_gm_le_on_family_scales — a tied family gives that upper bound with exponent 1/2 + cε — 546
Supply of tied families — shape_closed_link_n_of_green — the record and Green give a tied family for every small ε — 51,775
Supply of fields — supplyChi — VWin gives the hosts that the families live on — 3,488
A tied family is a family that satisfies the code's condition ChainTied, which the section on the wanted characters describes.
The structure ChainTie of the section on the chain is a different object.
This document calls shape_closed_link_n_of_green the shape theorem.
The definitions are in StatementOC.lean, Analytic.lean and ExplicitFormulaErrorOfHostConditions.lean.
Write Λ(n) for the von Mangoldt function and γ for Euler's constant.
The sum Sz x below has the order x·log x, and Gz x is that sum with its main terms subtracted.
Sz x is the sum of Λ(n)·(x/n − 1) over n ≤ x.
Gz x is Sz x − x log x + (1 + γ)x.
gChi χ y for a nontrivial character χ is the sum of Λ(n)·χ(n)·(y/n − 1) over n ≤ y, plus y times the logarithmic derivative of L(χ, s) at s = 1.
For a trivial character it equals Gz y.
A level holds a finite set KEPT of primitive characters, which contains the trivial character, and a natural number o.
The sum Gm y of the level is Gz y plus the real parts of gChi ψ y over the nontrivial ψ in KEPT, each with a positive weight.
The weight is 1/(3·o + 1), except for one optional character psK whose weight is 1.
formB states the step for every level.
Let 0 < θ < 1 and la > 1.
Suppose that for every bound there is a Y above it such that Gm x ≤ x^θ holds for all x between Y and Y^la.
Then the L-function of every character of KEPT, the zeta function among them, has no zero with real part above θ.
The condition asks only for an upper bound, and only on such intervals.
The proof of zero_free_all_of_green_v_win uses la = 3/2. zeroFreeAll_of_topG applies the step to every primitive character ψ separately.
It takes the level Level.cyc ψ of the powers of ψ, and the theorem Level.mem_cyc says that ψ is among the kept characters of that level.
formB reduces to zeroFree_of_rpow_window, which rests on 86 declarations.
The Landau reading read that proof, and this session read in full the lemma landau_tails that the reading had read by statement.
The account below has four stages and follows the report, except for stage 3.
Put g(u) = Gm(e^u).
Its Laplace transform Φ(s), the integral of g(u)·e^(−su) over u > 0, exists for real part above 2. Φ continues to real part above 0 with a simple pole at every zero of one of the L-functions.
The theorem poleData builds Φ from each character and its inverse, with half of the weight each.
The residue at a zero ρ is −S/(ρ(ρ − 1)), where S adds, for each character and for its inverse, half of the weight times the multiplicity of ρ as a zero of its L-function.
The weights are positive, so S is positive and the pole stays when two characters share a zero.
A growth bound |g(u)| ≤ C·e^(2u) is part of the same record of facts about g and Φ.
For σ > 2 and a real τ, the Taylor coefficient of order k of Φ at σ + iτ is (−1)^k times the integral of g(u)·u^k·e^(−(σ + iτ)u)/k! over u > 0.
The interval of x from Y to Y^la is the interval from U to (1 + δ)U in the variable u, with U = log Y and δ = la − 1.
On it the bound on Gm gives |g| + g ≤ 2R with R = e^(θu).
The integral of R·e^(−θu) over the interval is δ·U, which is below e^(ηU) for every η > 0 and large U, and the weight u^k·e^(−(σ − θ)u)/k! is at most (σ − θ)^(−k).
Together these bound the part of the integral on the interval by a multiple of e^(ηU)/(σ − θ)^k, for the sum of two quantities.
One is the norm of the integral at σ + iτ and the other is the integral at σ itself.
landau_tails handles the part of the integral outside the interval.
It picks σ from δ alone and the order k = ⌈(1 + δ/2)·σ·U⌉.
The lemma bounds the integral of the weight u^k·e^((2 − σ)u)/k! outside the interval by C/σ^k with a constant C that is the same for every U.
The factor e^(2u) of the weight comes from the growth bound of stage 1.
By this session's own calculation, which the Lean text does not state, the weight peaks at u = k/(σ − 2), and that point lies inside the interval when σ is above 4(1 + δ)/δ and U is large.
On each side of the interval the proof multiplies the weight by an exponential factor that is at least 1 there and integrates over all u > 0.
Suppose a zero has real part above θ.
Stages 2 and 3 bound the sum of the norm at σ + iτ and the integral at σ by a multiple of e^(ηU)/(σ − θ)^k.
The proof splits into two cases.
In the first it picks the height τ so that one zero ρ is the only singularity nearest to σ + iτ, at a distance d below σ − θ, and the integral at σ + iτ has norm about c/d^k.
By the report a disc around σ with a radius e above d holds no singularity in this case, and a Cauchy estimate keeps the integral at σ above −M/e^k.
In the second case the nearest singularity of σ is a real zero at a distance d below σ − θ, and its positive residue makes the integral at σ about c/d^k, while the norm at σ + iτ is at least 0.
In both cases c/d^k is at most M/e^k plus a multiple of e^(ηU)/(σ − θ)^k, with d below e and e at most σ − θ.
The order k grows in proportion to U, so for a small η the left side outgrows the right side, and the two contradict each other for large U.
The hypothesis enters once for each large U, so one interval for each Y of an unbounded sequence suffices.
By the report the proof uses Mathlib's analytic continuation of the L-functions and their nonvanishing for real part at least 1, and no functional equation.
The lemmas landau_pole_asym, landau_cauchy, landau_nearest and landau_finite, which carry stage 4, were read by statement.

sections.title: The wanted characters inside an auxiliary field

sentences.text: core_gm in CoreGm.lean proves the main inequality at one point x, and level_gm_le_on_family_scales applies it on the intervals. core_gm rests on 440 declarations, and this session read its statement and its proof.
For a level and all large x it takes a host and two conditions on the host.
The conclusion is Gm x ≤ x^(1/2 + (eD + eL + 7)·ε), where eD and eL are two constants of the conditions.

The statement ChebyshevInequalityAtWindowScale in TopWin.lean asks for eD and eL first and for every small ε after them, so the exponent is 1/2 + c·ε with a constant c that depends on neither ε nor Y.
The condition CoreAtH is an existence statement with 23 witnesses and sixteen conditions.
It says that a record Data of real numbers exists over the host with the condition SizeData₂ of the next section and fifteen further conditions.

ChainTied is the form of the same statement for a family, with four further conditions that tie the numbers of the record to the data of the family, and tiedCore_of_chainTied passes from it to the form for a host.
The condition EAtH concerns the characters and has six fields.
Its field kept places the characters of the level among the characters of the host.

It says that every character of the level is the primitive character that induces some character of the host from a set Xp. That set holds the characters of the host that are trivial on the image of a subgroup A0 in the Galois group of the host and take the value 1 at one element iod of that Galois group.
The code calls a character of the host kept when a character of the level induces it.
A second set Xm holds the characters that are trivial on A0 and take the value −1 at iod.
The field bdG speaks about the set Bounded, which holds the characters of Xp that are not kept and all characters of Xm.
The field asks that every primitive Dirichlet character χ that induces one of them satisfies ‖gChi χ x‖ ≤ x^(1/2 + ε) at the point x of core_gm.
This document calls the characters of Bounded the other characters.
A field bdL asks for a bound on their logarithmic derivatives at 1.
The field bdG is a bound of square-root size for the other characters, so its source matters. cone.py --users lists sigA_le as the one constant that mentions the field.
That theorem, which rests on 108 declarations and was read by statement, bounds a sum SigA of prime sums, which the subsection on ch_core defines, by 4·o·x^(1/2 + ε).
cone.py --users also lists one theorem that mentions the constructor of the record EAtH, which is supplyOfAdmOf in supplyOfAdmOf.lean.
It rests on 1,964 declarations, supplyChi reaches it, and this session read its proof in full.
The theorem works with the level of the powers of one primitive character ψ and takes three premises.
They are a statement that supplies a host from a pair of primes with PairGood, the bound of VWin for ψ, and a statement that supplies the ranks of a host.
This document does not record where the proof gets the condition TwistForm of the next sentences.
The proof fills bdG from the theorem boundedTw, and boundedTw reads it off the condition PairGood in PairGood.lean. boundedTw takes a condition TwistForm on the host.

It says that every character of the host that is trivial on A0 agrees with a power of ψ times the quadratic characters of q and d, each to the exponent 0 or 1, and that its value at iod is 1 when the exponent of d is 0 and −1 when it is 1.
A character of Xm has the exponent 1 of d.
A character of Xp has the exponent 0 of d, and when its exponent of q is 0 as well it agrees with a power of ψ, and the powers of ψ are the kept characters of this level.

A character of Xp that is not kept therefore has the exponent 1 of q, so every character of Bounded has at least one of the two quadratic characters present. boundedTw applies PairGood at the one argument y = x, where the bound y^(1/2 + ε/2) of that condition is at most x^(1/2 + ε).
The host depends on two primes q and d.
The condition WinPair fixes them for a parameter Y.
The logarithm of q lies between Y^(ε/5)/2 and Y^(ε/5), the logarithm of d lies between Y^(ε/5)·(log Y)²/2 and Y^(ε/5)·(log Y)², q divides d + 1, and every odd prime up to Y^(ε/5) divides d + 1.
PairGood speaks about the characters of a modulus M, multiplied by the quadratic characters of q and d with at least one of the two present.
For the level of the powers of ψ the modulus M is the modulus of ψ.

The field bounds says that every primitive character that induces such a product satisfies ‖gChi χ y‖ ≤ y^(1/2 + ε/2) for every y between Y and an upper end X, and that its logarithmic derivative at 1 is at most 4·log y in absolute value. pairEx proves the condition with X = Y^A, for an exponent A ≥ 1 that the caller chooses.
A further field boxes gives a zero-free box for the products in which the character of modulus M is replaced by a real character whose modulus divides 8·M.
pairEx proves that such a pair exists for every large Y, and it rests on 1,271 declarations.
It takes the pair from pair_exists, which takes it from pair_share.

That theorem states that both ranges hold primes, that all but a share η of the primes q in the first range meet a condition GoodQ, and that for each such q all but a share η of the primes d in the second range meet a condition GoodD. pair_exists applies it with η = 1/2.
This session read the statement of PairGood and read in full the proofs of boundedTw, pairEx and pair_exists.
The subsection on the pair of primes at the end of this section follows the proof of pair_share.
The logarithms of q and d are both at least Y^(ε/5)/2 once log Y ≥ 1, so for each fixed exponent B both primes exceed Y^B once Y is large.
The argument y of the field bounds is at most Y^A, which is at most (2·log q)^(5A/ε).
The field bounds therefore concerns sums whose length is at most a fixed power of the logarithm of the modulus.
That observation follows from the ranges above and is this session's own.
One of the sixteen conditions of CoreAtH is ThinScales.
It concerns the prime sums at arguments far above x, and it says that each of them is at most y·θ in absolute value for every y from a third of a bound X′ on, with two free numbers X′ and θ.
The statement PropTwoSixThinScales is a second statement of that shape, for a datum.
For every character χ of the host it has the conclusion ‖gChi χ y‖ ≤ y·exp(−c·x^(ε/8)) for y at least exp(x^(ε/3))/3 and a constant c, under a premise PropTwoSixBoxHypothesis on the host.
The code derives PropTwoSixThinScales from three statements that it bundles as LitThin and that litThin in LitThin.lean proves.
The first, adm6, holds a bound of a constant times Q^(1/4) on the number of zeros with real part at least 1 − 1/400 and the classical zero-free region with one possible exceptional real zero.
The second, adm7, is a truncated explicit formula.
The third, adm11, bounds the number of zeros in each window of height 2 by a constant times a logarithm. litThin rests on 319 declarations.
This session read the three statements, and it read neither their proofs nor the derivation of ThinScales from them.
pair_share in PairShare.lean rests on 1,239 declarations.
It is the source of the bound of square-root size for the other characters of the host.
Its files lie in the folder MeanSquareBounds, and the definitions that it uses lie in PrimeSetTwoBounds.lean and SecondEstimateOfIntervalHypothesis.lean.
The statement names two sets of primes and three conditions.
Write (n/q) for the Jacobi symbol of n and q, and Λ(n) for the von Mangoldt function as before.
primePairSetFirst of a number z is the set of the primes q with q ≡ 3 mod 8 and exp(z/2) < q ≤ exp(z).
The theorem takes z = Y^(ε/5).
primeSetTwoBounds of z, z′ and q is the set of the primes d with d ≡ 7 mod 16 and exp(z′/2) < d ≤ exp(z′) for which q and every odd prime up to z divide d + 1.
The theorem lets z′ lie between Y^(ε/5)·(log Y)² and K² times that number. pairEx takes z′ = Y^(ε/5)·(log Y)², which gives the range of d in WinPair.
Box is a condition on a character ψ with parameters Q, C, τ, Y and X, and it has three parts.
The first part, GoodC, says that ψ is nontrivial, that its modulus is at most Q and that L(ψ, s) has no zero with real part above 1 − 1/400 and imaginary part between −Q and Q.
The code calls the last property ZeroFreeBox.
The second part says that the logarithmic derivative of L(ψ, s) at s = 1 is at most C·log Y in absolute value.
The third part is the bound of square-root size, ‖Gchi ψ y‖ ≤ y^(1/2 + τ) for every y from Y to X.
GoodQ says about a prime q that Box holds with Q = N₀·exp(z) for every primitive character that agrees with ξ(n)·(n/q) at every n coprime to N₀·q, for every character ξ of a fixed modulus N₀.

GoodD says about two primes q and d that Box holds with Q = N₀·exp(z + z′) for every primitive character that agrees with ξ(n)·(n/d) or with ξ(n)·(n/q)·(n/d) at every n coprime to N₀·q·d, for every such ξ.
Gchi has the formula that the section on the prime sum gives for gChi of a nontrivial character, and a lemma in the file of pairEx proves that the two are equal.

pair_share states that a constant C exists for which the following holds for every ε below 1/52, every τ > 0, every K ≥ 1, every η > 0, every modulus N₀, every large Y, every X up to Y^K and every z′ of the range above.
The first set of primes is nonempty, and at least the share 1 − η of its primes q meet GoodQ.

For each of those q the second set is nonempty, and at least the share 1 − η of its primes d meet GoodD. pair_exists, which rests on 1,242 declarations, applies the theorem with η = 1/2 and takes one q and one d. pairEx applies pair_exists with τ = ε/2, K = A and N₀ = 8·M, and it turns the result into the fields of PairGood.
It takes the bound 4·log y on the logarithmic derivative from a further theorem, kappa4.
The proof of pair_share calls two theorems, stage1 for q and stage2 for d, which rest on 1,225 and 1,231 declarations.
Each of them states that the primes of its set that fail the condition form at most the share η of the set.
Both are cases of one theorem, stage, which rests on 1,219 declarations.
stage treats the set PPset of the primes p with p ≡ a₀ mod m₀ and √U < p ≤ U.
Its condition admitted asks that 8 divides m₀, that a₀ is coprime to m₀, that log U lies between Y^(ε/6) and Y^(ε/5)·(log Y)², and that (log Y)²·log m₀ is at most 4·log U.

A further premise asks that every prime factor of m₀ is at most Y^(ε/5) or above Y^(400K). stage1 takes m₀ = 8, a₀ = 3 and U = exp(Y^(ε/5)). stage2 takes U = exp(z′) and m₀ = 16·oddM, where oddM is q times the product of the odd primes up to z, and a lemma supplies a class a₀ for which primeSetTwoBounds equals PPset. stage2 applies stage with 6ε/5 in place of ε, so that the upper limit of log U covers every admitted z′.
stage takes a finite set of at most R primitive characters ξ whose moduli are at most a number F ≤ √U.
It calls a prime p of PPset bad when, for one of those ξ, the primitive character that agrees with ξ(n)·(n/p) fails Box with Q = F·U and X = Y^K.
It concludes that the bad primes form at most the share η of PPset.
The proof sorts the bad primes into two kinds and bounds each kind by the share η/2.

A bad prime of the first kind has a primitive character of modulus f·p, with f ≤ F, that fails ZeroFreeBox. count_bad, which rests on 89 declarations, bounds the number of such primes by a constant times (F·U)^(1/4), which is at most U^(3/8).
Its proof calls count_bad_core, which takes the bound from zero_density_box.

That theorem rests on 85 declarations and states that at most a constant times Q^(1/4) primitive characters of modulus up to Q have an L-function with a zero in that box. count_a, which rests on 19 declarations, concludes from the condition admitted that PPset holds at least U^(9/10) primes, and stage passes the prime number theorem in progressions and the bound excBound of the next list to it.
The share of the first kind is therefore at most a constant times U^(−21/40), which falls below η/2 once Y is large, because log U is at least Y^(ε/6).
A bad prime of the second kind has a truncated sum that is too large.

The code's sum S is the sum of Λ(n)·min(1, y/n)·ξ(n)·(n/p) over the n up to Z = Y^(400K), and the prime is of the second kind when the absolute value of S exceeds y^(1/2 + τ)/2 for some y from Y to Y^K. bad_share, which rests on 18 declarations, bounds the share of such primes for one ξ by η/(2(R + 1)).
The at most R characters together give at most R·η/(2(R + 1)), which is below η/2.
For a prime of neither kind box_of_S, which rests on 174 declarations, proves Box, so the prime is not bad.
box_of_S passes from the truncated sum to Gchi.
The identity finite_splitting_of_group, which rests on 7 declarations, writes Gchi ψ y as minus the truncated sum minus y times a tail tailL.

The tail is minus the logarithmic derivative of L(ψ, s) at s = 1 minus the sum of Λ(n)·ψ(n)/n over the n up to Z. tailK, which rests on 160 declarations, bounds Y^K times the tail by Y^ε for a character that meets GoodC.
Since y is at most Y^K, y times the tail is at most Y^ε, which is at most y^(1/2 + τ)/2 for ε ≤ 1/4 and Y ≥ 16.
With the truncated sum at most y^(1/2 + τ)/2 in absolute value the identity gives the third part of Box. kappaC, which rests on 164 declarations, gives the second part.
The number 400 appears twice, as the width 1/400 of the zero-free box and as the exponent of the truncation point Z = Y^(400K).
This session read tailK by statement.
It is this session's guess that the tail is small because a zero-free box of width 1/400 gives a saving of Z^(−1/400), which equals Y^(−K).
bad_share takes a mean square bound as its premise, the code's MeanSq.

That premise says that the sum of |S|² over the primes p of the set is at most a constant C₂ times y·log y times the number of those primes, for every y of the interval and every sequence of coefficients of absolute value at most 1 in place of ξ.
A prime of the second kind has |S|² above y^(1 + 2τ)/4 at some y.
The proof cuts the interval into blocks from 2^i·Y to 2^(i+1)·Y.
Write V for the left end of a block.
Inside the block the proof bounds |S|² at any y by twice |S|² at V plus 2V times the integral over the block of the square of the right-hand derivative of S in y.
That derivative times y is the sum S with the coefficients of the n ≤ y set to 0, so the premise bounds both terms, and their sum over p is at most 4·C₂·V·log(2V) times the number of primes.
Each prime of the second kind adds at least V^(1 + 2τ)/4, and log(2V) is at most 2·V^τ/τ, so the share of the block is at most (32·C₂/τ)·V^(−τ).
The sum over the blocks is at most the geometric series (32·C₂/τ)·Y^(−τ)/(1 − 2^(−τ)), which falls below every positive share as Y grows.
meanSqK, which rests on 1,100 declarations, proves MeanSq for PPset on the interval from Y to Y^K.
It combines two theorems.
meanSq_abs, which rests on 51 declarations, multiplies the square out.
The sum of |S|² over p is at most a sum over pairs n, n′ of weights times the absolute value of the sum of (n/p)·(n′/p) over p, because the coefficients have absolute value at most 1.
The proof rewrites that absolute value as the absolute value of the sum of (p/r) over p, where r is the product of the primes outside m₀ that divide n·n′ to an odd power.
For the pairs with r = 1, which are the pairs for which n·n′ is a square up to primes of m₀, it uses the trivial bound by the number of primes.
Those pairs include the diagonal n = n′, and their weights add up to at most a constant times y·log y.
For every other r but one it takes as a premise that the absolute value of the sum of (p/r) over p is at most a factor η′ times the number of primes.
The pairs of the one excepted r get the trivial bound as well, and their weights also add up to at most a constant times y·log y.
twistK, which rests on 1,021 declarations, supplies that premise.

It states for all exponents A′ and B′, every large Y and every U, m₀ and a₀ that meet admitted that each odd squarefree r > 1 that is coprime to m₀ and at most Y^(A′), with one possible exception, has a sum of (p/r) over the primes p of PPset whose absolute value is at most Y^(−B′) times their number. meanSqK uses it with A′ = 800K, because r is at most n·n′ ≤ Z², and with B′ = K + 1, so the factor η′ is Y^(−(K + 1)).

The proof of twistK starts from four statements. pnt_progressions_relative_weak_holds, which rests on 982 declarations, is the prime number theorem in arithmetic progressions with a relative error and one possible exceptional real zero. zFRDirichlet, which rests on 201 declarations, is the zero-free region of the L-functions of one modulus with at most one real zero in it. excBound, which rests on 136 declarations, says for every δ > 0 that a real zero of the L-function of a real nontrivial character of modulus N is at most 1 minus a constant times N^(−δ). page_across, which rests on 6 declarations, says that two real characters of moduli up to a bound W that each have a real zero close to 1 agree wherever both are defined, which is why one exception is enough.
This paragraph is this session's interpretation of the mechanism, except for the sentence on abs_pair_sum_eq, which reports a statement.
A prime p of PPset exceeds √U, and the logarithm of U is at least Y^(ε/6), so p exceeds Z², the largest value of n·n′, once Y is large.

The lemma abs_pair_sum_eq shows that the sum of (n/p)·(n′/p) over the primes p of a fixed residue class modulo m₀ has the same absolute value as the sum of (p/r) over them, for the number r of the item on meanSq_abs, and (p/r) is a real character of p. That character is nontrivial unless n·n′ is a square up to primes of m₀, and the prime number theorem in progressions makes the sum of a nontrivial character over the primes small.
On average over p the values (n/p) for different n therefore cancel as independent signs do.
The sum S has about y/log y terms up to y that are not zero, one for each prime power, and each has size about log y.
With independent signs its square is about (y/log y)·(log y)², which is y·log y.
The truncated sums have square-root size for most primes p of the set for that reason, and the proof then fixes one prime q and one prime d for which they have it.
The third part of Box speaks about the y from Y to Y^K only, a range far below the modulus.
This session found no statement about zeros in Box other than the zero-free box of GoodC.

This session read in full the proofs of pair_share, stage1, stage2, stage, box_of_S, count_bad, count_bad_core, meanSq_abs, meanSqK and bad_share with the five lemmas that precede it in its file and carry the blocks.

It read by statement zero_density_box, count_a, tailK, kappaC, finite_splitting_of_group, abs_pair_sum_eq and the four statements that the proof of twistK starts from, and it read the first sixty lines of the proof of twistK.

sections.title: From the two bounds on the slope to the exponent 1/2

sentences.text: Two theorems carry the main inequality.
This session read both proofs in full, without all the lemmas that they call.
Neither proof contains a theta lift or a lattice.
The lifts appear as m copies of one term and as real numbers in a record.
ch_core in ChCore.lean rests on 177 declarations.
It works with the characters of a finite abelian group E0 × H that stands for the Galois group of the host.
Each character ψ has a prime sum GPsi, which has the form of gChi with a function that the theorem takes as data in place of the logarithmic derivative.
ASK is a sum over the odd primes p up to a bound P, other than two primes q1 and d of the host, whose Frobenius class lies outside a set of classes, the code's PhiSet.
The code calls those primes inert.
Each of them adds 2·log p times a sum, over the powers p^i, of the positive parts max(a/p^i − w, 0), where w is a positive weight that depends on the class of p^i.
A similar term with log d is added for the prime d.
MAIN is the term that ASK is compared with, the expression a·(log a − 1 − γ + L − W).
Here L is the value of the function of GPsi at one character, and W is the mean of log w over PhiSet.
The number a is a number a t for each element t of a finite set TT, and a condition SizesA keeps every a t / b within 1 of x, for a scale b of the record.
The weights w belong to an element u0 of the group H and to a lift j, so ASK and MAIN depend on t, u0 and j.

The theorem assumes the bound that ch_top proves for ASK − MAIN, summed over TT and over the m lifts, for every u0 in the subgroup A0 of H, and it takes twelve conditions on sizes, windows and characters.
It concludes that GmA, a weighted sum of the real parts of the prime sums of the kept characters, is at most x^(1/2 + (C + 3)ε) plus SigA.

SigA is the sum of the absolute values of the prime sums of the characters that are trivial on A0 and not kept, and C is a constant that the caller chooses. core_gm bounds SigA with sigA_le of the section on the wanted characters and passes from GmA to the sum Gm x of the level.
Row — Lemma — What it does — Rests on
1 — ch_balance — proves the exact identity ASK − MAIN = De by orthogonality of characters — 67
2 — th_le — moves every prime sum inside De to one common argument — 55
3 — core — sums over a subgroup A0, which removes every character that is nontrivial on it — 134
4 — one_char — replaces the sum over TT by the value at x — 16
5 — proposition_size_bound — divides by the size of the sum and reads off the exponent — 9
This session read the lemmas of rows 2 to 4 in full and those of rows 1 and 5 by statement, and it read the lines of the proof of row 5 that carry the exponents.
De is one over the size of PhiSet times a double sum, over the classes g outside PhiSet and the characters ψ of E0 × H, of the conjugate of ψ(g) times a weight w times GPsi of ψ at a/w.
Row 1 is therefore finite Fourier inversion between primes in classes and character sums, and it holds for a > 0, positive weights on PhiSet and P ≥ a/w.

Row 3 takes the bound Err of ch_top and a number g that is at most the mean over TT of the real part of a sum of the GPsi, with values of the characters as coefficients, over the characters that are trivial on A0.
It concludes nT·m·b·((nT2/n)/2)·g ≤ Err + 2·nT·m·b/x, with the sizes nT, nT2 and n that the next paragraph names.
Row 2 bounds one quantity from above by ASK − MAIN of a lift plus 2·b/x.
That quantity holds no weight w, so it is the same for every lift j, and the sum over the m lifts multiplies it by m.
Row 4 uses a premise on the set TT.
The sum of a nontrivial kept character over TT differs from its expected value by at most a constant times x^(−1 + ε) times the size of TT.
Row 5 divides the error by nT·m·b times half of the ratio nT2/n.
Here nT is the size of TT, n is the size of the group H and nT2 is the size of a second set T2.
The error is x^(Cε) times the expression errorBracketSizeWindows, which is the sum nT·aE·(1 + m²/k) + m·(B + N), where B stands for 2·n·m·b·x^ε and N for nT2·k·b·x^(2ε)/n².

The condition BNBounds in SChain.lean says that B and N bound two numbers B0 and Nc of the record of the next subsection, and the error terms of the condition DIV of that subsection contain nT * a * La and m * (B0 + Nc).
The condition RestSize bounds aE by 2·x·b, n/nT by 2·x^(ε/8) and k by n²·x^(1/2 − ε), and it gives x^(1/2 − ε) ≤ m and x^(−ε) ≤ nT2/n.
Here aE is the scale a of the record and k is the number k of the ranks of the datum, which this subsection uses in that one meaning.
The theorem assumes m ≤ x^(1/2 + ε/2) and x·m ≤ k, and nT2 ≤ n holds because T2 is a subset of H.
The list below divides the bracket by nT·m·b alone, and by this session's own arithmetic that division leaves four terms.
The part nT·aE gives aE/(m·b), which is at most 2x/m.
The premise x^(1/2 − ε) ≤ m of RestSize keeps it below 2·x^(1/2 + ε).
The part nT·aE·m²/k gives aE·m/(k·b), which is at most 2 because x·m ≤ k.
The part m·B gives 2·n·m·x^ε/nT, which is at most 4·m·x^(9ε/8).
The premise m ≤ x^(1/2 + ε/2) keeps it below 4·x^(1/2 + 13ε/8), the exponent that appears in the proof.
The part m·N gives nT2·k·x^(2ε)/(n²·nT), which is at most 2·x^(1/2 + 9ε/8) because nT2 ≤ n, n/nT ≤ 2·x^(ε/8) and k ≤ n²·x^(1/2 − ε).
The four terms add up to at most 10·x^(1/2 + 13ε/8).
The ratio nT2/n is at least x^(−ε) by RestSize, so the division by half of it costs a further factor of at most 2·x^ε.
With the factor x^(Cε) of the error and a last factor x^(3ε/8) that absorbs the constants, the exponent is 1/2 + (C + 13/8 + 1 + 3/8)·ε, which is 1/2 + (C + 3)·ε.
proposition_size_bound of row 5 proves the code's statement GrowthSizeBound.
The premise of that statement is the conclusion of row 3 with G − 4·x^(1/2 + ε) in the place of g.
Besides the error of the four terms it holds two small terms.
Its error side holds 2·nT·m·b/x besides the error, and the division turns that into at most 4·x^ε/x.
Its other side holds a real number G lowered by 4·x^(1/2 + ε).
The exponent of the conclusion absorbs both for large x, and the statement asks for 26 ≤ x^(3ε/8).
GrowthSizeBound is a statement about any real number G, and ch_core applies it to GmA − SigA.
Its conclusion G ≤ x^(1/2 + (C + 3)·ε) is therefore the bound for GmA with SigA added.
The first term falls as m grows, and the third term grows with m.
Without the factors x^(cε) they are x/m and m, which are equal at m = √x, the chain length that the note gives.
The proof does not choose m.
It takes x^(1/2 − ε) ≤ m ≤ x^(1/2 + ε/2) as premises, and the fourth term has the size of about √x for every m, because k is at most n²·x^(1/2 − ε).
The first term comes from the part of the error that carries no factor m, so the m lifts share it.

The third comes from the number B0, which enters once for each of the m lifts and which is itself a multiple of m. core_gm calls ch_core with the constant C = eD + eL + 3, for which ch_core gives the exponent 1/2 + (C + 3)·ε, and its own conclusion has one ε more.
B0 and Nc are budgets that the code defines by formulas, in DataArith.lean and DataParams₂.lean.
For a datum, B0 is the number sizeBudget, the product f·m·b·x^ε, where b is exp(x^ε) and f is twice a number of the datum, written n′ in this paragraph.
The product has the form of the B of this subsection, and budgetNc, which is Nc, has the form of the N, each with n′ in place of n.
The condition BNBounds bounds B0 and Nc by the B and the N of this subsection.
The conditions of the next subsection then bound errors by multiples of B0.
One of them, EComp5, speaks about a number Ee of the record, which is a sum of one number for each of the m lifts.
It says that Ee differs from m times a product of two numbers of the record by at most a constant times m·B0.
B0 contains the factor m by its formula, so the factor m of the third term is part of the definition of the budget.
The reason why the errors of the m lifts fit m times a budget that itself grows with m lies in the proofs of those conditions, which this session did not read.
One premise of stepE_num, the theorem of the section on one lift, shows why the budget has to grow with m.

The field NumFacts.sw of its bundle of premises says that the shift w of lift j, which the next subsection identifies with the weight w of ASK, is at least the number s of the section on one lift, which is (k + (2j − 1)(t + 1))/2.
The lower bound for the shift grows with j, and the error term of that section grows with w.
ch_top in ChTop.lean proves the assumption of ch_core.
It bounds ASK − MAIN, summed over TT and the lifts, by x^(Cε) times the expression errorBracketSizeWindows that the subsection on ch_core writes out.
Here C is the code's CErr, which is eD + eL + 3. ch_top rests on 90 declarations.
Its premise SizeData₂, defined in SChain.lean, is a conjunction of eleven conditions on a record Data of 39 real numbers and real-valued functions from MeanBoundSecondForm.lean.
The theorem takes four further premises.
IdentU ties numbers of the record to the arithmetic data of ch_core.

It sets the field aT to the numbers a t, the field w to the weights of ASK, a field gam to γ, a field LpL to the real part of the value L of MAIN, and the field ASK of the record to the sum of ASK over TT and the lifts.
ErrWindows and LargeX are conditions on sizes, and BNBoundsU is the form of BNBounds for this record.
The record has three indices.
An index u0 runs over a finite set, which for a family is the set of the elements of the group H.
For each u0 an index u runs over a finite set that depends on u0.
An index t runs over a set in bijection with TT, and a field aT t equals the a t of ch_core.
The numbers muCC and Fo depend on u0 alone, and the numbers muN, h and T depend on u0 and u.
The bullets below fix one u0 and leave it out of the notation.
The number Main of the record stands for the sum of MAIN over TT and the lifts.
The code writes ph y for y log y − y.
Two of the eleven conditions hold the idea.
DIV bounds a number muCC from above.
For every u it says that muCC + h u − Fo is at most the sum over t of m * (ph (aT t) − aT t * logOm) − aT t * log (T u), plus error terms.
Here logOm is a constant that the section on one lift describes.
Among the eleven conditions this is the one in which the number m of lifts multiplies the main term.
SlopeIneq bounds muCC from below.
It says that the mean over u of muN u − h u with weights d u, minus the logarithm of the number of indices u and minus correction terms, is at most muCC.
The statement holds when three numbers of the record lie in stated ranges and a number HH is positive and at least that mean minus a number muMinCC.
The condition HHBound gives HH those two properties and bounds it from above by a power of x times b.
The condition FParams keeps the three numbers below three bounds of the record.
Two further conditions bring in ASK.

QuotientSlopeBoundsWith says for every u that muN u is at least a quantity Ga of u0 plus Fo, minus a number Ee of u and plus further numbers of the record, and LossBounds says that ASK is at most Ga plus a loss.
The theorem each_unit_bound_statement, which rests on 58 declarations, takes all eleven conditions and concludes that ASK is at most Main plus an explicit error.

Its proof has two lemmas. s_lower5 adds DIV to the bound of QuotientSlopeBoundsWith for each u, which cancels Fo and gives a lower bound for muN u − h u, and takes the mean over u with the weights of SlopeIneq.
It uses Count5 for the logarithm of T u, EComp5 for the number Ee and a condition Slopes for one further number.
It concludes that the mean s of muN u − h u is at least Ga + muCC minus two numbers, the main term of DIV with its errors and a mean of further errors.
Ga_bound5 adds SlopeIneq, by which s is at most muCC plus the logarithm and the corrections.
The two bounds for s cancel muCC.
With the identity of the next paragraph, Ga is at most Main plus the logarithm and errors.
By LossBounds, ASK is then at most Main plus errors.
This session read the proof of s_lower5 and checked by hand that the leftover terms add up to Main.
The reading of six proofs read Ga_bound5 in full and found the same cancellation of muCC.
The rest of ch_top shows that the errors fit inside the bound.
It calls core_ineq, an inequality between real numbers whose proof has about 10,000 characters, of which the reading of six proofs read the beginning.
Two definitions and an identity show how the main term of DIV becomes Main.
The record has a positive number w for each lift and each place.
A place of the record is an index that runs over a set in bijection with PhiSet, and v is a positive number of the record.
The condition Count5 says that the logarithm of the number T u is at least the sum over the lifts of the mean over the places of log(w·v/π), plus m times a number lg, minus an error.
It also bounds that logarithm from above and bounds how much it varies between the indices u.
The number Main holds, for each lift and each index t, the product of aT t and the sum log aT t − 1 − gam + LpL − ℓ, where ℓ is the mean over the places of log w.
The record defines logOm as gam + log(π/v) − LpL.
By IdentU the field gam is γ and the field LpL is the real part of the value L of MAIN.
The lemma key_identity5 proves the identity that carries the main term of DIV to Main.
With the lower bound of Count5 in place of log T u, the main term of DIV equals Main minus m times the sum of the aT t times lg, plus an error, and the two logarithms of π/v cancel in it.
The condition EComp5 then matches m times that sum times lg with the number Ee of the record.
IdentU ties the number w of the record to the weights w of ASK, and the tie TieArith gives those weights as the number wj of the datum, which is the number e of the lift at the place.
The shift w of the section on one lift has the same definition.

sections.title: The upper bound for the lattices of a datum
What the numbers of the record are

sentences.text: The eleven conditions speak about real numbers without saying what they measure.
The condition TieLocal in TieGlobal.lean says it for a family.
A map pt assigns a datum of the family to each element u0 of the group H, and the index u of the record runs over the words of that datum.
The bullets give four of the ties of TieLocal, for the datum of one u0.
The condition ties further numbers of the record, among them Fo, T u and Ga, to numbers of the datum that this document did not open.
muCC is the slope of the dual of a Hermitian lattice div.RR of the datum.
muN u is the slope of a lattice div.Nu u, one for each word, and the weight d u is the rank of that lattice.
h u is the number div.h u of the datum.
The datum has a linear map div.Bk u from Nu u into the dual of RR, and the condition WordFacts in RecBridge.lean requires that the height htMap of a nonzero Bk u is at most h u.
The number of lifts is the field R.m of the datum.
The definition lifts sets the set of lifts to Finset.Icc 1 D.R.m.
The slope inequality of step 5 is therefore about the maps Bk u of the words of one datum into one lattice.
The next subsection shows that the bound h u for the height of each map is a sum over the m lifts, which is how m enters.

sections.title: The path of the divisibility inequality

sentences.text: For the lattices of a datum the inequality says that the dual slope of RR plus h u minus Fo is at most a main term plus error terms, and the main term contains m times a sum of ph (aT t) over TT.

IsRecT, the notion of a local Langlands map in Row, constrains the map on GL₁ and on twists of depth-zero representations over the field ℚ_g of g-adic numbers.

AwayB, the comparison of Row at a place away from l, has three clauses.
It asks for equal dimension, for equality of the two objects in a torsion case, and for equal characteristic polynomials in a tame case.
This session confirmed the three clauses in the source.
The usual local-global compatibility asks for an isomorphism at every such place.

For δ below 1/2 the textbook proofs of that bound yield no value of c(δ). stage and twistK pass excBound to count_a, so if the size of Y from which count_a holds depends on c(δ), the proof yields no value of that size either.
